q: A diffraction grating is an optical device which consists of a large number of parallel slits of same width separated by equal opaque spaces.
e: True. Maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda, same as Young. Red diffracts at a larger angle than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. A grating is many equal parallel slits with equal opaque gaps, N lines per unit length, d = 1/N.

q: A diffraction grating is an optical device which consists of a large number of parallel slits of different widths separated by equal opaque spaces.
e: False. A grating uses parallel slits of the same width, separated by equal opaque spaces. Mixed widths would spoil the regular maxima. Equal pitch is the point of N lines per centimetre.

q: A diffraction grating can disperse light into its wavelength components.
e: True. A grating is many equal parallel slits with equal opaque gaps, N lines per unit length, d = 1/N. Maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda, same as Young. Red diffracts at a larger angle than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating.

q: A diffraction grating can disperse light into its intensity components.
e: False. A grating disperses light into wavelength components, a spectrum, not into intensity components. Intensity is how bright a colour is, not what the grating sorts. Spectroscopy is that wavelength split.

q: Diffraction grating is thus widely used as dispersive elements in spectrographic instruments and a crucial tool in the study of atomic and molecular compositions.
e: True. Maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda, same as Young. Red diffracts at a larger angle than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. Diffraction grating is thus widely used as cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: Diffraction grating is thus widely used as reflective elements in spectrographic instruments and a crucial tool in the study of macroscopic compositions.
e: False. Gratings are dispersive elements in spectrographs, used to study atomic and molecular composition, not macroscopic makeup. Reflection is only one grating type. Dispersion, not mere reflection, is the job.

q: Two types of grating are transmission grating and reflection grating.
e: True. Red bends more than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. Echoes follow the laws of reflection: angle in equals angle out. A large hard wall sends a countable repeat; many walls make reverberation.

q: Two types of grating are transmission grating and absorption grating.
e: False. The two types are transmission grating and reflection grating. Absorption grating is not the partner class. A compact disc is a familiar reflection grating.

q: The number of lines (or slits) per unit length is called the grating constant.
e: True. N is lines per unit length and d = 1/N; maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda. Red bends more than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. A single slit spreads light into a wide central maximum of width 2 lambda D / a.

q: The number of lines (or slits) per unit area is called the grating constant.
e: False. Grating constant N is lines per unit length, not per unit area. Then d = 1/N. Area would mix a second dimension that the formula does not use.

q: The condition for maximum intensity is the same as that for a Young's double slit.
e: True. Two slits make Young's straight fringes. Many equal slits make a grating with sharp principal maxima. Sound intensity is power per unit area, in W m^-2.

q: The condition for maximum intensity is different from that for a Young's double slit.
e: False. The grating maximum condition is the same as Young's: d sin theta = m lambda. Neighbouring slits still need an integer number of wavelengths of path difference. The grating just has many slits, not a new rule.

q: For maximum intensity to be formed at P, the path difference of two waves from adjacent slits is equal to an integral number of wavelengths.
e: True. It is not a sideways gap. m lambda is in phase; (m+1/2) lambda is out of phase. Maximum intensity to be formed at P cannot be dropped from this process without changing the law.

q: For maximum intensity to be formed at P, the path difference of two waves from adjacent slits is equal to a half-integral number of wavelengths.
e: False. A grating maximum needs an integral number of wavelengths of path difference from adjacent slits. Half-integral is a minimum. Same rule as Young's bright fringe.

q: If the number of slits per unit length is $N$, $d$ is equal to $N$.
e: False. If N is slits per unit length, d equals 1/N, not N. More lines per centimetre means smaller spacing. Setting d = N would invert the grating equation.

q: In the first order diffraction spectrum, longer wavelength (red light) diffracts at a greater angle than shorter wavelength (violet light).
e: True. Reflection is a bounce; this is spreading. Wavelength sets fringe spacing, diffraction angles and colour order on a grating. Longer lambda, larger angle in d sin theta = m lambda, so red sits farther out than violet.

q: In the first order diffraction spectrum, shorter wavelength (violet light) diffracts at a greater angle than longer wavelength (red light).
e: False. In the first-order spectrum, red, the longer wavelength, diffracts at a greater angle than violet. d sin theta = m lambda, so bigger lambda means bigger theta. Violet sits closer to the zero-order white.

q: A compact disc is an example of reflection gratings.
e: True. N is lines per unit length and d = 1/N; maxima still follow d sin theta = m lambda. Red bends more than violet in a given order; a CD is a reflection grating. A compact disc is a reflection grating: shiny tracks disperse colours.

q: A compact disc is an example of transmission gratings.
e: False. A compact disc is a reflection grating: its shiny tracks bounce and disperse colours. Transmission gratings send light through carved transparent lines. You see CD rainbows by reflection.

q: A reflection grating is a shiny surface having many fine grooves.
e: True. A large hard wall sends a countable repeat; many walls make reverberation. A reflection grating uses shiny grooves instead of openings. A diffraction grating is many equal slits with equal opaque gaps.

q: A reflection grating is a transparent surface having many fine grooves.
e: False. A reflection grating is a shiny surface with many fine grooves. Transparent carved lines are a transmission grating. Light bounces off the shiny grooves to form the spectrum.
